images.alt: A Xerox Alto minicomputer cabinet beside its keyboard, mouse, and tall portrait-format bitmap display
images.caption: The Alto's cabinet held a full minicomputer's worth of logic, wheeled up beside a desk rather than housed in a machine room.
images.author: Maksym Kozlenko

images.alt: A Xerox Alto workstation with its tall portrait monitor, keyboard, and three-button mouse on a desk
images.caption: Desk, chair, keyboard, mouse, and a screen shaped like a page: the Alto's whole claim was that a computer could look like this.
images.author: Unknown

images.alt: A Xerox Alto system with its processor cabinet, portrait display, keyboard, and mouse set up together
images.caption: About two thousand Altos were built at Xerox PARC and given away inside the company and to a handful of universities; none were ever sold.
images.author: Joho345

images.alt: A preserved Xerox Alto on display, showing the processor cabinet and portrait monitor
images.caption: A surviving Alto, decades later: the machine that first put overlapping windows, a mouse, and Ethernet in front of one person at a desk.
images.author: Don DeBold

images.alt: Close-up of the Xerox Alto's five-key chorded keyset, a separate input device beside the keyboard
images.caption: Beside the keyboard sat a five-key chorded keyset, borrowed from Doug Engelbart's oN-Line System, for issuing commands with one hand.
images.author: Vincent Lextrait
